title: Ms. Knope Goes To Washington

jokes.text: Andy smells 'the sweet sugar of bureaucracy at work' while standing outside the Capitol
jokes.setup: Leslie sets up a reverent, patriotic moment — 'you can practically smell the bills becoming laws'
jokes.punchline: Andy mirrors her earnestness with 'You can taste the sweet sugar of bureaucracy at work' — a perfectly nonsensical echo that reveals he has no idea what bureaucracy means but is performing enthusiasm
jokes.explanation: Andy's deadpan mimicry of Leslie's civic reverence — using an absurd phrase like 'sweet sugar of bureaucracy' — is perfectly character-integrated. Only Andy would mean this sincerely. Good economy, lands immediately.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: The Capitol building is a symbol of everything that's great about this country. The dome, the marble columns, the sense of history and importance...

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: It looks like a really big penis.

jokes.text: Andy: 'That building looks like a boob.' Leslie: 'Yeah, well, it's not.' Andy: 'Oh yeah, I know. It's the White House.' Leslie: 'No. It's the Capitol.'
jokes.setup: Andy makes an immature observation about the Capitol dome's shape, then attempts to demonstrate he actually knows what it is
jokes.punchline: He confidently misidentifies it as the White House — compounding the childishness with ignorance
jokes.explanation: A two-beat joke: the immature 'boob' observation sets up a recovery that immediately collapses. The structure is tight and the double-layer of Andy's confidence-in-wrongness is perfectly on-brand. Strong economy — lands in three lines.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: Wait, the Capitol building looks like a boob.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: It doesn't look like a boob, Andy.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: The dome is totally a boob. You're telling me the founding fathers built a giant boob in the middle of our nation's capital and nobody noticed?

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: That's not... that's not what it looks like.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: What about the Washington Monument? That's obviously a... you know.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: A what?

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: A giant... it's phallic, Leslie. Our capital is basically a dirty joke.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Andy, those are architectural landmarks that represent—

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: And the Lincoln Memorial? Two giant stone legs. Very subtle, guys.

jokes.text: Leslie: 'Now, throw it away, because Leslie Knope is your guidebook.' Andy throws the book away immediately. Leslie: 'I didn't mean literally. I had some notes in it.'
jokes.setup: Leslie delivers a grand metaphorical proclamation about herself as a guide
jokes.punchline: Andy takes it literally and discards the physical book; Leslie's immediate deflation reveals she did actually need it
jokes.explanation: A classic two-beat structure: grandiose setup punctured by Andy's literal-mindedness, then further punctured by Leslie's admission she had notes in it. Both characters land perfectly. The comedy of deflation plus Andy's chaos is very well constructed.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: I'm like your guidebook.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: Oh, okay.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: Then I don't need this anymore.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: *throws away actual guidebook*

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: No, no, no, Andy!

jokes.text: Leslie: 'Did I also just walk past a food truck and buy myself a waffle sundae? Yes!'
jokes.setup: Leslie is asking herself 'Am I living the dream?' in her talking head.
jokes.punchline: The waffle sundae is presented as coequal evidence of living the dream alongside meeting senators and cleaning up rivers — food is genuinely aspirational to Leslie.
jokes.explanation: Perfectly Leslie — waffles are almost a running character trait for her across the series. Her sincere, unironic joy at the waffle sundae as a life achievement is endearing and funny. Character integration is high because it ties into a show-wide bit. Docked slightly for not landing a particularly sharp punchline beyond the food revelation itself.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: The National Mall is one of the most historic parks in the country.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: Wait, there's a mall? I need to go get some flip-flops.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: No, Andy, it's not a shopping mall. It's a national park.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: Oh. Well, that's disappointing.

jokes.text: Andy: 'There's a mall? That's awesome. I need to get some flip-flops.'
jokes.setup: Leslie says 'let's hit the National Mall' — a famous Washington landmark
jokes.punchline: Andy hears it as a shopping mall and immediately plans a purchase
jokes.explanation: A quick wordplay/misdirection gag on 'mall.' Not original — this is a well-worn joke setup — but the specificity of 'flip-flops' is a nice Andy character touch. Functional and fast.

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: I'm throwing the annual barbecue.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: You mean the Pawnee Harvest Festival Celebration Barbecue Extravaganza?

jokes.text: The fact that Ron is running the conference room meeting in Leslie's absence — presented as extraordinary
jokes.setup: Donna explains in talking head: 'Ron has taken initiative and is leading the meeting'
jokes.punchline: Donna's tone treats this as a minor miracle, implying Ron normally does absolutely nothing
jokes.explanation: Solid character-based setup — the joke is entirely in Donna's framing of a basic managerial act as remarkable. Works as a running joke about Ron's legendary inertia but is a relatively soft laugh.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: ♪ Parks and Rec, it's the best in the laaand ♪

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: ♪ You gotta fill out Form 27-B before you use the sand ♪

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: ♪ Submit it in triplicate, notarized and signed ♪

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: ♪ Leave it at the office, we'll review it in time ♪

jokes.text: The full name: 'the Leslie Knope Employment Enjoyment SummerSlam Grill Jam Fun-splosion'
jokes.setup: Ron says he'll throw the annual barbecue; someone asks if that includes all of Leslie's traditions
jokes.punchline: April rattles off the absurdly long official name of Leslie's event — with 'SummerSlam' and 'Fun-splosion' as the highlights — revealing the baroque excess of Leslie's planning
jokes.explanation: The name itself is the joke — an escalating cascade of Leslie-isms that perfectly captures her over-engineered enthusiasm. 'Fun-splosion' is a genuinely funny invented word. Character-integrated and quotable.

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: I don't understand why we need all these activities. We have meat. We have fire. We cook the meat on the fire. That's a barbecue. Everything else is just... noise.

jokes.text: Tom listing Leslie's barbecue activities: 'the popsicle-eating contest, the slip-and-slide-a-thon, the watermelon carving, the gazpacho-off'
jokes.setup: Ron has agreed to run the barbecue in Leslie's absence.
jokes.punchline: The list of activities Tom recites escalates from normal summer fun to 'the gazpacho-off' — a weirdly specific, upscale cold-soup competition that is completely incongruous with a public parks barbecue.
jokes.explanation: 'Gazpacho-off' is the key word — it's the comedic peak of the list. The escalation from popsicle-eating to an artisan cold-soup competition is absurd and perfectly in Leslie's character. The joke rewards attention to the list structure.

dialogue.speaker: Jerry
dialogue.line: Can I bring corn to the barbecue?

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: No. Corn is a vegetable.

jokes.text: Parks and Dolls — April sings an original song about park rules and regulations
jokes.setup: A list of Leslie's elaborate barbecue traditions culminates in 'and star in a one-woman show about parks rules and regulations'
jokes.punchline: April actually performs a snippet of the song ('I got your park right here / Its name is Ramsett Park...') with complete deadpan commitment
jokes.explanation: The show committing to an actual original song about parks regulations — with rhyme and meter — is a delightful level of effort. The absurdity of Leslie writing a musical about her own department, and April performing it straight, earns the laugh.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: Whoa, whoa, whoa! This could be a treasure map!

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Andy, that's gum.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: Gum that's been here for like a hundred years. That makes it old gum. Old things are valuable.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: It's literally just gum stuck to a monument.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: A monument to treasure hunting!

jokes.text: Ron's barbecue manifesto: 'no foofy desserts... no giant soap bubble guns... no adult men in costumes... and most of all, no vegetables'
jokes.setup: Ron is contrasting his stripped-down barbecue with Leslie's elaborate one
jokes.punchline: The escalating list of prohibitions — culminating in 'no vegetables' as the most sacred prohibition — is pure Ron Swanson philosophy rendered as absurdist policy
jokes.explanation: This is quintessential Ron Swanson — the escalating list of banned items where 'no vegetables' is treated as the gravest offense, on par with or surpassing the others. The structure is perfect: each item slightly more absurd, with the vegetable prohibition as a philosophical statement. 'Most of all, no vegetables' is instantly quotable and deeply character-integrated. Earns the 8.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: And this is the Washington Monument, built to honor our first president, George Washington. It's one of the most iconic structures in our nation's capital.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: It's a big... you know.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Yes, Andy, it's a monument.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: No, I mean it's like a giant... it's a big ol' dong.

jokes.text: Tom: 'Well, Ron, can we at least have corn on the cob?' Ron: [beat] 'No.'
jokes.setup: Ron has banned all vegetables from the barbecue; Tom asks about a classic American staple
jokes.punchline: Ron's single flat 'No' after a beat — corn on the cob being a vegetable in Ron's worldview — is perfectly delivered deadpan
jokes.explanation: The callback to the vegetables rule lands perfectly. Maximum economy — one word does all the work. The humor is in Ron's absolute consistency and the implication that corn on the cob, America's most innocuous barbecue item, is as unwelcome as a kale salad. Near-perfect economy score.

dialogue.speaker: Chris
dialogue.line: You're doing great, Ron! That's perfect form! The way you're holding that spatula is really inspiring! Keep it up!

dialogue.speaker: Chris
dialogue.line: Ron? Ron, did you hear me? I said your form is inspiring!

dialogue.speaker: Chris
dialogue.line: He can't hear me, can he? He's like fifty yards away.

jokes.text: Andy treats gum on the Lincoln Memorial as a National Treasure-style clue
jokes.setup: Andy is excited about the Lincoln Memorial; he spots something and says 'A-ha! A clue.'
jokes.punchline: It's just gum. He refuses to accept this. 'How do I know this isn't a treasure map just waiting to be unfurled?' Leslie: 'Because it's gum. That's gum. Yeah.'
jokes.explanation: Andy's National Treasure fixation is well-established character comedy. The beat of Leslie having to say 'it's gum' three times while Andy remains unconvinced is a good extended rhythm. Leslie's straight-man exhaustion sells it.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: Wait, the pig's name is Tom?

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: Yes. It's a coincidence.

jokes.text: Andy about the Washington Monument: 'Leslie, this is a really cool penis but Ben and April are meeting us at the Smithsonian in 10 minutes.'
jokes.setup: Leslie is giving a serious, informative explanation of the Washington Monument's construction history — color changes, halted construction
jokes.punchline: Andy cuts her off with 'this is a really cool penis' — delivered with complete sincerity and zero malice — then pivots to logistics
jokes.explanation: This is one of the episode's best jokes. The structure is excellent: Leslie's earnest, detailed historical lecture is punctured by Andy's sincere, non-malicious acknowledgment of the obvious phallic shape — and then he immediately moves on to scheduling. The deadpan pivot to 'Ben and April are meeting us at the Smithsonian in 10 minutes' makes it perfect. Only Andy can say this with zero irony. Earns the 8+.

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: Now children, gather around. I'm going to show you how we turn this pig into delicious meat. First, we need a sharp knife and a steady hand. You see, when you slit the throat, you want to cut deep and quick so the pig doesn't suffer. Then we'll hang it up by the hind legs and let all the blood drain out into this bucket. Next comes the fun part—we scald it in boiling water to remove the hair and skin. Then we use this cleaver to split open the belly and remove all the organs. Each one has a specific purpose. The liver, the kidneys, the heart—all delicious. And don't worry about the squealing sound it makes, that's just air escaping from the lungs. Who wants to help me gut it?

jokes.text: Chris watching Ron's barbecue from afar, yelling 'Way to be, Ron! You're really getting it done, man!' then quietly: 'He can't hear me.'
jokes.setup: Chris is watching Ron set up the barbecue from a distance
jokes.punchline: Chris cheers enthusiastically in Ron's direction, then flatly notes to himself that Ron cannot hear him — but continues to find it meaningful
jokes.explanation: Classic Chris Traeger — relentlessly positive even when alone, even when meaningless. The self-aware acknowledgment 'He can't hear me' without changing his behavior is perfectly character-integrated.

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: It's not a real permit, just my libertarian philosophy written down.

jokes.text: Ron reveals the pig to the barbecue guests: 'Everyone? Meet your meat.'
jokes.setup: Barbecue guests expect a normal cookout; Ron emerges with a live pig
jokes.punchline: 'Meet your meat' — the pig is named Tom (same as a coworker), Ron is going to slaughter it on-site
jokes.explanation: 'Meet your meat' is a brilliantly economical phrase — a wordplay pun that also delivers Ron's entire philosophy about food, death, and the circle of life. It's immediately quotable, perfectly Ron, and sets up the subsequent pig-Tom name coincidence. One of the episode's most memorable lines. Earns the 8+.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: Hey, you know what? You're doing a great job. Really impressive work here.

dialogue.speaker: Security Guard
dialogue.line: Oh, uh... thanks?

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: No, seriously. The way you stand there, the alertness, the uniform. You're like a human sentinel.

dialogue.speaker: Security Guard
dialogue.line: Well, I appreciate that.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: Which is why I have to ask — where are you hiding the treasure maps?

dialogue.speaker: Security Guard
dialogue.line: What? I'm not hiding anything.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: A guy as thorough as you? A museum this old? There's definitely treasure maps. And you know where they are.

jokes.text: The pig is named Tom. 'Burn.' — everyone reacts to the coincidence with the human Tom Haverford.
jokes.setup: Ron introduces the pig: 'His name is Tom'
jokes.punchline: Someone says 'Burn.' — the implication that naming the slaughter pig after Tom Haverford is a deliberate insult; Ron insists it's his 'given Christian name'
jokes.explanation: The coincidence of the pig sharing Tom Haverford's name, Ron's stone-faced insistence that it's the pig's 'given Christian name,' and the ensemble 'Burn' reaction creates a layered joke. Ron's deadpan defense ('I understand that it's hilarious. But that is his given Christian name.') is excellent character work — he would never acknowledge the joke, which makes it funnier.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Oh my gosh, we should go to the Ritz-Carlton and get spa treatments, and then we can hit up the Natural History Museum, and then—

dialogue.speaker: April
dialogue.line: We're going to sit in the hotel room and watch TV.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: What? No, April, we have so much to see and do!

dialogue.speaker: April
dialogue.line: I'm aware of what exists, Leslie. I choose not to experience it.

jokes.text: Ron: 'Tom is very smart and incredibly loyal. He's basically a dog. A dog we're going to cook, chew, and swallow.'
jokes.setup: Ron is humanizing the pig Tom to the horrified guests
jokes.punchline: He pivots from warm description ('basically a dog') to cold culinary fact ('a dog we're going to cook, chew, and swallow') without any tonal shift
jokes.explanation: This is peak Ron Swanson. The pivot from 'basically a dog' to 'a dog we're going to cook, chew, and swallow' is a perfect deadpan escalation — three verbs (cook, chew, swallow) adding increasing intimacy to the act. Only Ron would say this without irony or cruelty, just matter-of-fact carnivore philosophy. Earns the 8+.

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: Goodbye, April.

dialogue.speaker: April
dialogue.line: Hey, Ben? Your eyes are on my butt.

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: What? No, they're not.

dialogue.speaker: April
dialogue.line: They are. It's okay. But they are.

jokes.text: Ron to a child: 'Which one of you youngsters wants to help me drain the blood from this animal? If you do a good job, I'll give you the bladder. You can blow it up for a fun play ball.'
jokes.setup: A guest points out there are kids around; Ron takes this as an opportunity to involve them
jokes.punchline: Ron's child-appropriate version of butchering involves draining blood and offering the bladder as a balloon — delivered as a genuine reward for good behavior
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's best jokes. The setup — 'there are kids around' — normally signals moderation. Ron instead sees it as an opportunity for youth education in frontier skills. The bladder-as-play-ball detail is specific, historically accurate (kids did this), and utterly horrifying in a suburban park context. 'If you do a good job' as incentivized child labor in butchering is inspired. Deeply character-integrated, highly quotable, genuine originality.

dialogue.speaker: Jerry
dialogue.line: I'm exhausted. I walked all the way from the parking lot.

dialogue.speaker: Ann
dialogue.line: Jerry, that's like fifty feet.

dialogue.speaker: Jerry
dialogue.line: I know. My dogs are barking. I need to sit down.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: Just sit on the ground.

dialogue.speaker: Jerry
dialogue.line: On the ground? With all this dirt and... groundness?

jokes.text: Ron's permit reads: 'I can do what I want.' He presents this to the official as a legitimate permit.
jokes.setup: An official challenges Ron's pig slaughter at a public park; Ron says he has a permit
jokes.punchline: The permit simply states 'I can do what I want' — Ron wrote it himself as Parks Director and treats it as legally binding
jokes.explanation: A near-perfect Ron Swanson joke. The permit reading 'I can do what I want' is the Platonic ideal of Libertarian Ron logic — he is the Parks Director, this is a park, therefore his self-issued permit is valid. Maximum economy (five words on the permit), maximum character integration (only Ron), highly quotable. One of the episode's top three jokes. Earns the 8+.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: That's not a picnic blanket, that's a Hermès throw.

jokes.text: Ron concedes, then as he leads the pig away: 'Let's go, Tom.' Immediately corrects himself: 'No. Pig Tom.'
jokes.setup: Ron has been insisting the pig's name Tom has nothing to do with Tom Haverford
jokes.punchline: He instinctively calls the pig 'Tom' — the same name as the coworker — then distinguishes with 'Pig Tom,' implying the human Tom is 'Regular Tom'
jokes.explanation: The callback earns its place. Ron's self-correction to 'Pig Tom' implies he routinely uses this distinction — meaning the pig predates this conversation and the name was always going to be an issue. Excellent economy and a satisfying button on the pig-Tom running gag.

dialogue.speaker: Donna
dialogue.line: So what are we?

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: We're Tomna.

dialogue.speaker: Donna
dialogue.line: No.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: Donnom?

dialogue.speaker: Donna
dialogue.line: No.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: Ton?

jokes.text: Andy climbs on a train in the Smithsonian and asks if it's from Back to the Future III
jokes.setup: Leslie is trying to see historical exhibits; Andy immediately turns the Smithsonian into an adventure
jokes.punchline: Andy has climbed on a museum artifact and is connecting it to a movie — the gap between tourist and destructive child is played physically
jokes.explanation: Solid Andy physical comedy — his inability to behave in a museum is on-brand. The Back to the Future III reference is funny but not exceptional. Works as a visual gag dependent on performance.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: We're doing this. We're moving in together. Right now.

dialogue.speaker: Ann
dialogue.line: Tom, we've known each other for like three hours.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: Exactly. So we better lock this down before you come to your senses.

dialogue.speaker: Ann
dialogue.line: I'm going to come to my senses in like five minutes.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: Then we have to sign the lease before that happens.

dialogue.speaker: Ann
dialogue.line: We can't sign a lease right now. We're drunk.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: Even better. We won't remember how stupid this is.

jokes.text: Andy to the security guard who removes him from the train: 'Sir, you protect our nation's history and you're a hero. Yeah. A hero with something to hide. Like probably a treasure map.'
jokes.setup: A museum security guard has just told Andy to get down from an exhibit
jokes.punchline: Andy sincerely compliments the guard, then immediately pivots to accusing him of hiding a treasure map — completing his National Treasure delusion
jokes.explanation: The callback to National Treasure lands well. Andy's transition from genuine hero-worship to conspiracy accusation in two sentences is perfectly of-a-piece with his character. The guard's visible frustration (inferred) adds to the beat.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: Look, I need this. My credit is shot, my car payment is three months behind, and I'm pretty sure my landlord is going to evict me. So yes, we're staying together.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: At least until I can figure out how to tell my mom that I'm not actually engaged anymore. She already posted about it on Facebook.

jokes.text: Ben and Leslie reuniting — awkward extended hug while April watches, then Ben and April exit to have sex, leaving Andy and Leslie visibly uncomfortable
jokes.setup: Leslie and Ben reunite after being apart; the reunion kiss/hug goes on longer than comfortable in front of April and Andy
jokes.punchline: April, with zero filter: 'We were going to have sex.' Andy tries to smooth things over with 'astronaut ice cream' — the couple has no interest
jokes.explanation: April's blunt 'We were going to have sex' is the punchline — completely unfiltered April honesty cutting through the awkward PDA. The cringe of Andy trying to redirect with 'astronaut ice cream' adds another layer. April's delivery is signature character comedy.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: My stomach's doing that thing again. That... growly-wowly noise.

jokes.text: Leslie: 'George Washington's Farewell Address Candle Stand.' Ben: 'That was the first thing I was going to see.' Leslie: 'God, I love you so much.'
jokes.setup: Ben and Leslie briefly share a moment before his meetings; Leslie starts to recommend a sight
jokes.punchline: Ben finishes her obscure historical reference perfectly — both of them are nerds who would know and care about the Farewell Address Candle Stand, and they recognize it as romantic
jokes.explanation: A warm character joke that simultaneously characterizes both Leslie and Ben as history nerds and their relationship as built on shared nerdiness. The joke works on multiple levels — it's funny because of how obscure 'Farewell Address Candle Stand' is, and sweet because they both care about it.

dialogue.speaker: Chris
dialogue.line: What should we give the kids to drink at the barbecue?

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: Water it down beer. Why waste good beer on kids when you can just give them water?

jokes.text: Ben telling Leslie what to see: 'George Washington's Farewell Address Candle Stand.' Leslie: 'That was the first thing I was going to see.'
jokes.setup: Ben is rushing off and tries to recommend a sight for Leslie.
jokes.punchline: He recommends something so hyperspecific — the candle stand associated with the Farewell Address — and Leslie immediately confirms it was her top priority. They are perfectly matched nerds.
jokes.explanation: A delightful couple joke — the comedy is that these two people are so perfectly nerdy that 'The Farewell Address Candle Stand' is a completely normal thing to say. Their instant alignment on this obscure artifact is genuinely sweet and funny. High character integration: this joke only works with Ben and Leslie.

dialogue.speaker: Ron Swanson
dialogue.line: When you grill a steak, you're not just cooking meat. You're engaging in an ancient ritual that connects you to your ancestors, to the land, to the very essence of what it means to be alive. The sizzle of fat hitting hot iron, the smoke rising like incense to the gods of carnivore heaven. You caress the meat with your tongs like you're touching the skin of a lover. You whisper to it. You tell it that everything is going to be okay.

jokes.text: Ben: 'And it was nice to see you again.' Leslie: 'Were you talking to my butt?' Ben: 'Yes.'
jokes.setup: Ben politely says goodbye to April and Andy as well as Leslie; Leslie suspects his farewell was directed elsewhere
jokes.punchline: Ben's immediate, unashamed 'Yes' — no hesitation, no embarrassment
jokes.explanation: Quick and effective — the single-word punchline 'Yes' with no defensiveness is charming and gets a laugh. Not particularly original but well-timed and efficiently delivered.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Ben and I are like the Obamas, or the Clintons, or any other power couple in history. We even have a signature dance move.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: *demonstrates an awkward dance move*

jokes.text: Tom: 'Ann, I'm hungry and my legs are tired. It feels like I just exercised.'
jokes.setup: The Pawnee group is at the barbecue; Tom is complaining about standing
jokes.punchline: 'It feels like I just exercised' — Tom's definition of exhaustion is merely standing still at an outdoor event
jokes.explanation: Classic Tom Haverford — his absolute physical fragility and aversion to anything resembling effort. The comparison to exercise for simply standing is perfectly calibrated to his character.

dialogue.speaker: Receptionist
dialogue.line: You fill out the form, wait six to eight weeks, and we'll review your application.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Yeah, but I'm going to get it done in like two weeks because I'm going to call you every single day and bring you waffles and find out what your favorite song is, and then I'm going to write it on the form so when you see my application you'll be like, 'Oh, this girl gets me.'

jokes.text: Jerry: 'Just sit on the ground.' Tom: 'No, Jerry. It's dirty and I'm wearing my summer linens.'
jokes.setup: Tom is complaining about having to stand.
jokes.punchline: 'I'm wearing my summer linens' — Tom's refusal to sit on the ground because of his outfit, delivered with complete seriousness.
jokes.explanation: 'Summer linens' is a good specific fashion reference that works for Tom, but this is a fairly standard 'Tom is fussy about his clothes' joke. Solid execution with high character integration, but not especially original.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: I've prepared a multimedia presentation for this grant application. It includes a 47-minute interpretive dance sequence, a holographic recreation of our town's founding, and a original song cycle performed by the Pawnee Community Theater.

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: Leslie, it's a $500 grant application.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: I know. That's why I kept it simple.

jokes.text: Tom and Ann's talking-head reveal: they broke up after day one of moving in together but are faking being together to win a bet
jokes.setup: Everyone assumes Tom and Ann ('Haverkins') are going strong; we cut to their talking head
jokes.punchline: They reveal the relationship collapsed immediately but they're maintaining the fiction — Tom to win a $1,000 bet with Donna, Ann just out of spite
jokes.explanation: A strong structural reveal — the episode has been treating this as a real relationship, then pulls the rug in the talking head. 'I can't stress this enough. If she finds out that we broke up, I'll go bankrupt.' as the stakes is very Tom. The drunken 'no take-backs' origin story is a nice compressed flashback beat.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: There are apparently eight different Pawnees.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: Yeah, there's Pawnee, Indiana, Pawnee, Oklahoma, Pawnee, Illinois...

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Okay, so my entire town's identity is completely generic.

jokes.text: Flashback: Tom and Ann drunkenly agreeing to move in together with 'No take-backs when we sober up, though, partner. No take-backs, partner.'
jokes.setup: Tom explains how they ended up agreeing to move in together
jokes.punchline: The 'partner' formality of the agreement and the explicit 'no take-backs' clause — a children's playground rule applied to adult relationship decisions while drunk
jokes.explanation: The 'no take-backs, partner' framing treats a major life decision with the gravity of a playground handshake. Both characters mirroring each other ('partner') is a nice touch. Funny character insight — this is exactly how Tom would approach a relationship decision.

dialogue.speaker: April
dialogue.line: You're fired. I'm taking your office.

jokes.text: Ron on giving children beer diluted with water: 'Why not just give the kids water?' 'I suppose you could do that.'
jokes.setup: A guest asks what the children can drink; Ron suggests watering down the beer
jokes.punchline: When someone points out the obvious alternative (just water), Ron treats it as a creative suggestion he hadn't considered — 'I suppose you could do that'
jokes.explanation: The joke is in Ron's worldview: water-downed beer IS the child-appropriate option in his mind; plain water is the unexpected innovation. His 'I suppose you could do that' is delivered as if considering an unconventional loophole. Perfect Ron character integration. Economy is excellent.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: Wait, so you're telling me I have to wear pants? Like, real pants?

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: But where am I supposed to get pants? Is there like a pants station or something? Do they just hand out free pants?

jokes.text: Ron's talking head: 'These people are soft. They're grill virgins. But by the time this day is over, they will have been taken by the grill and delicately and tenderly shown the ways of flavorful meat-love.'
jokes.setup: Ron is frustrated that his guests are complaining about waiting for food
jokes.punchline: Ron describes the barbecue experience in the language of a sensual seduction — 'grill virgins,' 'tenderly shown the ways of flavorful meat-love' — with complete sincerity
jokes.explanation: Ron Swanson applying romantic/sexual language to meat is inspired. 'Grill virgins' and 'meat-love' are both hilarious coinages, and 'delicately and tenderly' in the context of Ron's machismo is a perfect tonal collision. His earnestness makes it land — he's not being ironic at all. Highly quotable, earns the 8+.

dialogue.speaker: Jerry
dialogue.line: I've got some smuggled candy if you're hungry.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: Smuggled candy? Yes, please.

dialogue.speaker: Jerry
dialogue.line: It's raisins. Nature's candy.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: Jerry, raisins are just dried grapes. That's not candy, that's... that's just sad.

jokes.text: Ron's talking head: 'These people are soft. They're grill virgins. But by the time this day is over, they will have been taken by the grill and delicately and tenderly shown the ways of flavorful meat-love. The first time is so beautiful.'
jokes.setup: Ron reflects on the barbecue crowd's inexperience.
jokes.punchline: Ron applies the language of sexual initiation — 'grill virgins,' 'delicately and tenderly,' 'meat-love,' 'the first time is so beautiful' — to barbecue grilling, with complete sincerity.
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's best jokes. The extended metaphor of grilling as sexual initiation — 'grill virgins,' 'meat-love,' 'the first time is so beautiful' — is original, sustained, and deeply in character. Ron's reverence for meat is a well-established character trait, so the framing of grilling as a sacred, intimate initiation ritual is both surprising and completely consistent. 'Meat-love' is a coined word that deserves to exist. The delivery of 'The first time is so beautiful' as a sincere statement about grilling someone's first properly cooked meat is genuinely funny. Earns 8+.

dialogue.speaker: Ann
dialogue.line: Tom, there's glitter all over my clothes. What did you do?

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: Oh, that's my new business venture: Glitter Gal. We bedazzle your entire wardrobe while you sleep.

dialogue.speaker: Ann
dialogue.line: That's insane. What's your slogan?

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: Glitter Gal: Because you didn't ask for it, but you're getting it anyway.

jokes.text: Leslie talking head: 'Ben and I are a power couple, like the Roosevelts or the Clintons. I mean, the only way we could be more awesome is if we had our own signature dance move. Oh wait. We do.'
jokes.setup: Leslie is comparing herself and Ben to famous political power couples
jokes.punchline: She realizes mid-sentence they already have a signature couples dance move — as if this is a normal thing political power couples have
jokes.explanation: Leslie's self-mythologizing is always funny — comparing herself to the Roosevelts is on-brand. The pivot to 'we have a signature dance move' as the apex of power-couple status is absurd and specific to Leslie. The mid-sentence self-correction ('Oh wait. We do.') is a good structural choice.

dialogue.speaker: Ann
dialogue.line: You've got glitter condoms, glitter lube, glitter body spray...

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: Glitter toilet paper. The slogan is 'Leave a Sparkly Surprise.'

jokes.text: Leslie to the federal receptionist: 'I'm not most people.' — then the meeting turns out to be cancelled
jokes.setup: Leslie grandly announces she's not most people (who just mail applications in) — she's here for a face-to-face
jokes.punchline: The official stepped out for the day; she's told to add her application to the pile
jokes.explanation: The irony works well — Leslie's confidence punctured immediately by bureaucratic indifference. Her grandiose self-declaration setting up an immediate pratfall is a reliable structure that fits her character perfectly. The cringe of watching her absorb it is the secondary laugh.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: These little pigs in a blanket are amazing! And the crab cakes? Forget about it!

dialogue.speaker: April
dialogue.line: I know. I've been taking them all night.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: Wait, what? You're stealing them?

dialogue.speaker: April
dialogue.line: Not just the food. The plates too.

jokes.text: Leslie describes her CD with babbling river sounds and DVD with frolicking river otters that she planned to use in her presentation — now left in the pile
jokes.setup: Leslie is told to just leave her application in the pile with everyone else's
jokes.punchline: She begins describing the elaborate multimedia presentation she prepared — river sound CD, otter DVD — that will never be seen
jokes.explanation: The tragedy-comedy of Leslie's over-preparation meeting bureaucratic indifference. The river sound CD and frolicking otter DVD are pitch-perfect Leslie Knope details — she would absolutely make these. The cringe of watching her mention them to an uninterested receptionist is effective.

dialogue.speaker: Party Guest
dialogue.line: Local government is really important.

dialogue.speaker: Party Guest
dialogue.line: I see it as charity work for elderly people.

jokes.text: Receptionist listing all the states with a town called Pawnee: 'Is that Pawnee, Illinois, Indiana, Iowa, Kansas, Missouri, Nebraska, Oklahoma, or Texas?'
jokes.setup: Leslie says her application is for Pawnee
jokes.punchline: The receptionist rattles off eight states that have a Pawnee — making the town feel even smaller and more insignificant than Leslie thought
jokes.explanation: A nice observational gag — 'Pawnee' is a common enough name to require clarification, further deflating Leslie's sense of her town's importance. The sheer length of the list (eight states) escalates the joke nicely. Functional, well-placed.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Today I got mistaken for Jennifer Aniston at the grocery store.

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: That's nice.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: I know! I've accomplished so much.

jokes.text: Ben in his D.C. campaign office — Leslie immediately claims it as hers: 'Ben, you're fired. It's my office now. Boom! You heard the boss. Scram, Wyatt.'
jokes.setup: Ben shows Leslie his impressive D.C. campaign office
jokes.punchline: Leslie immediately takes it over, firing Ben, and having April back her up — Leslie's enthusiasm and sense of ownership kicks in immediately
jokes.explanation: Solid Leslie character moment — her immediate territorial impulse and April's gleeful 'Scram, Wyatt' supporting her are fun. Not exceptional but breezy and in-character.

dialogue.speaker: Chris
dialogue.line: What happened to those vegan soy patties I brought?

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: I gave them to some children to use as skipping stones.

jokes.text: Andy to Ben: 'Hey, Benjamin. How fancy is this party tonight? I mean, is it, like, a shorts or a pants kind of gala?'
jokes.setup: Ben announces a swanky D.C. cocktail party
jokes.punchline: Andy's frame of reference for formal events is whether pants are required — and he uses 'gala' correctly while asking about shorts
jokes.explanation: The juxtaposition of Andy correctly using 'gala' while asking if shorts are acceptable is a great Andy joke. His formal/informal register confusion is perfectly calibrated. 'Shorts or pants kind of gala' is a quotable construction.

dialogue.speaker: Jerry
dialogue.line: If you don't help me to the bathroom right now, I'm going to urinate in the trees.

jokes.text: Ben: 'Pants.' Andy: 'Great. Could we just real quick stop at the nearest place that has free pants?'
jokes.setup: Ben confirms it's a pants event; Andy accepts this immediately
jokes.punchline: Andy asks to stop for 'free pants' — he doesn't own dress pants and his solution is to find pants that cost nothing
jokes.explanation: The callback to the pants question lands with a good second beat. 'Free pants' as a category of pants (like a store that gives them away) is very Andy. His complete unselfconsciousness about being pants-less makes it charming rather than sad.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: I need some fresh air.

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: Leslie, we're outside.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: I need fresher air!

jokes.text: Jerry smuggled raisins to the hungry barbecue crowd: 'It's nature's candy. Now, they're basically grapes, so remember to pace yourself.' Then immediately: 'I can't even follow my own advice. They're so delicious.'
jokes.setup: Jerry heroically produces contraband food for the starving group
jokes.punchline: It's raisins. His claim that they're 'nature's candy' and advice to 'pace yourself' as if they're a controlled substance, then immediately breaking his own advice
jokes.explanation: Jerry treating raisins as an exciting contraband treat is wonderfully pathetic and warm. 'Nature's candy' plus 'they're basically grapes so pace yourself' is an absurdist nutritional warning. His immediate inability to follow his own advice about raisins is a perfect button. Underrated joke.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: These D.C. women are like Machiavelli in a pencil skirt. They smile while they're cutting you down, they network at charity galas, and they somehow make political betrayal look like it's from a Vogue photoshoot.

jokes.text: Tom has put glitter in the laundry detergent: 'SparkleSuds. Dress Loud.'
jokes.setup: Ann discovers glitter in her laundry detergent
jokes.punchline: Tom has branded it — 'SparkleSuds. Dress Loud.' — as a legitimate entrepreneurial venture
jokes.explanation: Tom's micro-entrepreneurship with a tagline ('Dress Loud') is pitch-perfect character work. The product is insane, the branding is real — this is exactly how Tom thinks. Good economy in the three-word tagline.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: We have a pothole the size of a small car, our parks are underfunded, and there's a duck that won't leave the community center pool. It's been there for three weeks and I think it might be planning something.

jokes.text: Tom has put glitter in the butter: 'Disco Dairy. Spread the Party.'
jokes.setup: Ann protests the laundry glitter; Tom reveals this is a pattern
jokes.punchline: 'Disco Dairy. Spread the Party.' — the butter has also been branded, escalating the absurdity
jokes.explanation: 'Disco Dairy. Spread the Party.' is a genuinely excellent three-word tagline joke. It escalates from the laundry detergent to reveal this is a systematic campaign, and the butter branding is funnier because butter is more intimate and more absurd than detergent. 'Spread the Party' is a legitimately great pun (spread as in butter). One of the episode's most quotable lines. Earns the 8+.

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: Hey, you know what? You're an amazing woman. You're smart, you're passionate, you care about people.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Thanks, Ben.

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: And you know what else? You're not alone. There are tons of amazing women out there doing incredible things.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Really?

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: Yeah. I mean, look at—

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: I have a list. Women I admire. It's numbered. I've been working on it since high school. I'm up to 247.

jokes.text: Tom: 'Well, the target demographic isn't angry, middle-aged nurses.'
jokes.setup: Ann (a nurse) protests Tom's glitter ventures as terrible ideas
jokes.punchline: Tom calmly explains she's not the target demo — with a very specific demographic description that perfectly describes Ann
jokes.explanation: The specificity of 'angry, middle-aged nurses' as a demographic category — delivered as a calm business analysis — is very funny. Tom isn't being cruel; he's doing market segmentation. The precision of the insult being framed as demographic research is excellent character comedy.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: Okay, okay, hear me out. 'Glitter Cheeks' — it's a blush that's 60% actual glitter.

dialogue.speaker: Jerry
dialogue.line: That sounds like a skin condition.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: The slogan is 'Sparkle Like You've Made Better Life Choices.'

jokes.text: Tom to Donna: 'We're good. We're really good. No, just spending a little time with my baby girl.' Ann: 'Ew. Get off me.'
jokes.setup: Donna asks if they want anything from the food line; Tom performs the happy couple
jokes.punchline: Tom's 'baby girl' endearment gets an immediate visceral 'Ew. Get off me.' from Ann — the performance cracking visibly
jokes.explanation: The fake-couple performance cracking under pressure of genuine revulsion is good cringe comedy. Ann's 'Ew' is instinctive and real. Functional joke in the ongoing fake-relationship subplot.

dialogue.speaker: Donna
dialogue.line: Oh, I know. Tom told me you two broke up. He was very upset.

dialogue.speaker: Ann
dialogue.line: Wait, when did he tell you that?

dialogue.speaker: Donna
dialogue.line: I don't know, a while ago. I lie about stuff all the time, so I can't really keep track of when people tell me things.

jokes.text: Ann and Tom's fake public display of affection: 'Oh, my God. You're so smart. Tom. You're amazing. Kiss me more. Uh-huh.'
jokes.setup: Donna approaches, and Ann and Tom must pretend to still be in a happy relationship.
jokes.punchline: Their performed affection is wildly over-the-top and unconvincing — 'Kiss me more. Uh-huh.' is hilariously mechanical.
jokes.explanation: 'Kiss me more. Uh-huh.' is funny in its mechanical, scripted quality. The cringe of watching two people perform fake romance is a familiar comedic situation, but the specific lines they use are appropriately terrible.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: I created a composite woman in my head. She's got Natalie Portman's face, Scarlett Johansson's body, and Michelle Obama's arms.

jokes.text: Ben proudly shows Leslie he got them on the list for a swanky party; Leslie makes a shrimp claw and asks Ben to put her used plate in her purse — she's building a collection
jokes.setup: Leslie is overwhelmed by the free food at the fancy political party
jokes.punchline: Leslie's response to a power networking event is to build a 'complete set' of used plates in her purse — treating it like a county fair rather than a D.C. event
jokes.explanation: Leslie's shrimp claw and plate-collecting reveal a charming dissonance — she's at a power cocktail party but she's still Pawnee Leslie at heart. 'I almost have a complete set' treats fancy party dishware like commemorative spoons. Character-specific and warm.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: Hey, look, I know you're upset about the merger, but think about it — it's like an amalgam of two great things coming together.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: That's... actually not a terrible way to look at it.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: Right? And you know what an amalgam is? It's like a llama, but with more letters. A-M-A-llama. I'm basically a genius.

jokes.text: D.C. woman condescendingly: 'Local government is so important. My grandma is on the city council in her town. It gives her a reason to leave the house.'
jokes.setup: Leslie introduces herself as a city councilwoman; the D.C. women respond with impressed-sounding statements
jokes.punchline: The 'compliment' reveals she sees local government as an old-lady hobby akin to bingo — something that gives grandma purpose
jokes.explanation: An excellent cringe joke. The woman means it as a compliment but the subtext ('like a hobby for old ladies') lands as a devastating dismissal of Leslie's life's work. The structure — genuine-sounding setup, slow-burn insult — is well-built. The audience's discomfort on Leslie's behalf amplifies the impact. Funny and emotionally resonant.

dialogue.speaker: Chris
dialogue.line: You know what? I've been forwarding around some really funny email chains about the puppet show.

dialogue.speaker: Jerry
dialogue.line: Oh, that's great!

dialogue.speaker: Chris
dialogue.line: Yeah, but then I realized I accidentally forwarded your entire financial portfolio to the whole office.

dialogue.speaker: Jerry
dialogue.line: What?!

dialogue.speaker: Chris
dialogue.line: And now everyone's been forwarding it around. It's become more popular than the puppet show emails.

dialogue.speaker: Jerry
dialogue.line: No, no, no...

jokes.text: Leslie's talking head: 'Ben and I both did some amazing things today. He scored a victory for the congressional campaign. And I was mistaken for Beverly D'Angelo by a Japanese tourist. So, pretty big day for both of us.'
jokes.setup: Leslie is tallying the day's accomplishments as a power couple
jokes.punchline: She presents being mistaken for Beverly D'Angelo as equivalent to a congressional campaign victory — and genuinely means it
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's best jokes. The structure is perfect: genuine parallel construction ('he did X, I did Y') where the Y is absurdly small by comparison but delivered with identical weight. 'Beverly D'Angelo' is a specific, funny choice — someone famous enough to name, obscure enough to be funny. Leslie's complete sincerity makes it land. 'Pretty big day for both of us' is a great button. Earns the 8+.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: Oh my god, is that a gun?

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Don't touch it, that's evidence.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: Finders keepers!

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: That's not how the law works.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: I'm calling it. This gun is mine now. I'm gonna name it Mr. Whiskers and we're gonna be best friends.

jokes.text: The D.C. party women condescend about Pawnee: 'My grandma is on the city council in her town. It gives her a reason to leave the house.' / 'Pawnee, Missouri, is a total crap-hole.'
jokes.setup: Leslie has just introduced herself as a city councilwoman from Pawnee, Indiana.
jokes.punchline: One woman compares her to a grandmother who uses council work to leave the house. Another confuses Pawnee with Pawnee, Missouri, and calls it a 'total crap-hole.'
jokes.explanation: Two-part joke that lands reasonably well. The grandmother comparison is a casual cruelty delivered without malice, which is a specific social register. 'Pawnee, Missouri, is a total crap-hole' is an unexpected geographical twist — the Pawnee name callback from the receptionist scene adds to the joke that Leslie's town is perpetually confused with inferior Pawneess. Good comic escalation.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: Welcome to the Washington Monument, folks. This thing was built in 1884, and it's the tallest structure in D.C. Fun fact: it's also where they filmed that awesome scene in Independence Day where the alien ship blows it up. Will Smith is so cool.

dialogue.speaker: Tourist
dialogue.line: Actually, the monument was completed in 1884, and Independence Day came out in 1996.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: Yeah, well, the point is it's really tall and stuff, and that movie had way more history in it than this building, to be honest. Next stop: the Lincoln Memorial, where Lincoln give his famous speech about, uh, doing stuff.

jokes.text: Ron: 'Ron, where are my vegan soy patties?' 'I gave them to the kids. They love them. They're skipping them across the pond.'
jokes.setup: An employee asks for their vegan option at the barbecue
jokes.punchline: Ron has given them to children to use as skipping stones — treating vegan food as inherently toy-like rather than edible
jokes.explanation: A brilliantly specific Ron joke. He hasn't destroyed the vegan patties — he's repurposed them as children's pond-skipping toys, which implies their natural state is as a flat disc rather than food. 'They love them' adds the detail that children are better suited to using soy patties than eating them. Near-perfect character integration. Earns the 8+.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: So the Oval Office is called that because it's shaped like an oval, right? But here's the thing - most people don't know the real origin story. It actually comes from Orville Redenbacher.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: See, JFK loved popcorn. Like, loved it. And Orville Redenbacher was his favorite brand. So one day, JFK is eating popcorn in the Oval Office, and a kernel pops and flies into his ear. And he's like, 'This office is shaped like a popcorn kernel!' So they renamed it the Oval Office. Oval like a popcorn kernel.

dialogue.speaker: Tourist
dialogue.line: That doesn't sound right.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: It's 100% true. I learned it at the visitor center.

jokes.text: Employee: 'I mean, how are we supposed to eat these rumps?' Ron: 'If no one takes me to the bathroom, I'm just going to have to go in the trees.'
jokes.setup: Employees are complaining about the barbecue — no plates, discomfort, poor planning
jokes.punchline: Jerry's complaint about bathroom access (he needs a ride in Donna's car) escalates to threatening to relieve himself in the trees, forcing Ron's hand
jokes.explanation: Part of the escalating barbecue complaints sequence. Jerry threatening to use the trees is the breaking point that finally gets Ron to cave — appropriate character beat. Not exceptional but functional.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: That was an amazing tour, Andy. Really incredible.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: Thank you! You know what, I'm going to start charging for these tours.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: Five thousand dollars per person.

jokes.text: Ron's reaction to the complaints: 'You have ruined a perfectly good barbecue with your demands and chatter.' — then he abandons his own party
jokes.setup: Ron has been holding out for his ideal barbecue while guests suffer; they finally break him
jokes.punchline: Ron blames THEM for ruining his barbecue — the barbecue he has refused to actually serve food at — and leaves
jokes.explanation: 'Demands and chatter' as the crime against the barbecue — when the demands were just food and bathrooms — is perfectly Ron. His righteous indignation at normal human needs is the joke. 'Perfectly good barbecue' for an event with no food is inspired irony.

jokes.text: Leslie at the party, increasingly overwhelmed: 'God, these women. They're so smart and accomplished and pretty. And they're tall. Why are they all so tall? It's like C-SPAN and Neiman Marcus had kids or something.'
jokes.setup: Leslie is surrounded by D.C. power women at the cocktail party and feeling intimidated
jokes.punchline: Her spiral lands on their height as the most inexplicable quality, then the 'C-SPAN and Neiman Marcus had kids' metaphor — a perfect collision of policy and fashion
jokes.explanation: 'C-SPAN and Neiman Marcus had kids' is a genuinely excellent simile — it captures the exact type of D.C. power woman in seven words. The escalating panic (smart, accomplished, pretty... but WHY are they tall) is well-structured. Leslie's specific frame of reference (C-SPAN and Neiman Marcus) is perfect for her character. Earns the 8.

jokes.text: Leslie meeting Senators Barbara Boxer and Olympia Snowe — her nervous self-deprecation spiral: 'We're small and unimportant... We've got tons of problems. We're overrun with raccoons and obese toddlers.'
jokes.setup: Leslie is introduced to two actual U.S. Senators — numbers 4 and 26 on her list of amazing women
jokes.punchline: She catastrophically oversells Pawnee's problems — 'raccoons and obese toddlers' — then immediately apologizes for boring them and retreats
jokes.explanation: 'Raccoons and obese toddlers' is a great Pawnee joke — specific enough to feel like a real town problem, absurd enough to be funny. Leslie's simultaneous hero-worship, self-deprecation, and inability to shut up is painful and perfect. The Senators' polite discomfort is the cherry on top. Strong character integration — this is Leslie at her most Leslie.

jokes.text: Ben reveals he arranged for Leslie to meet 'numbers 4 and 26 on Leslie's List of Amazing Women'
jokes.setup: Leslie is upset and deflated after the party; Ben tries to cheer her up
jokes.punchline: The reveal that he specifically cross-referenced Senators Boxer and Snowe against Leslie's ranked list of amazing women — and that such a numbered list exists — is both sweet and absurd
jokes.explanation: The joke is that Leslie has a numbered, ranked, comprehensive list of Amazing Women and Ben knows it well enough to engineer a specific meet-and-greet. This reveals both Leslie's obsessive list-making AND Ben's loving attention to it. Character comedy of the best kind — it's also romantically touching.

jokes.text: Leslie: 'You're the most amazing boyfriend ever. And if you don't get out of here soon, I'm going to punch you in the face.'
jokes.setup: Leslie is genuinely moved by Ben's gesture but is also emotionally overwhelmed
jokes.punchline: The threat of face-punching as an expression of overwhelming affection — stated matter-of-factly as if it's a natural consequence of being too sweet
jokes.explanation: The misdirection from genuine sweetness to face-punch threat is an efficient joke. Leslie's emotional regulation manifesting as violent threats is specific to her and the delivery sells it. Short and punchy (so to speak).

jokes.text: Ann puts glitter in all of Tom's moisturizers: 'SparkleSkin by Annie. Twinkle, Twinkle, Big Star.' Tom: 'Ann. That is an amazing idea and I will buy it from you. But never do that again.'
jokes.setup: Ann is retaliating for Tom's SparkleSuds/Disco Dairy by putting glitter in his products
jokes.punchline: Tom's response is to immediately see commercial potential and offer to purchase the intellectual property — even while telling her never to do it again
jokes.explanation: Tom's inability to not see business opportunity even in retaliation is excellent character comedy. 'I will buy it from you. But never do that again.' — the two clauses in complete contradiction — is a great two-beat joke. The callback to the glitter-branding running gag lands perfectly here with Ann accidentally creating something Tom wants. Earns the 8.

jokes.text: Donna reveals she knows Tom and Ann broke up: 'As someone who has lied a lot about various aspects of a myriad of relationships, I respect the effort you've gone to.'
jokes.setup: Tom and Ann are continuing their fake-couple performance; Donna sees through it immediately
jokes.punchline: Donna's reason for respecting them is her own extensive lying experience — stated with complete self-awareness and no shame
jokes.explanation: 'A myriad of relationships' that she's lied about — Donna's self-portrait as a veteran relationship liar is excellent. The dignity she confers on their effort ('I respect the effort') frames relationship deception as a craft. Very Donna.

jokes.text: Tom: 'The end of a relationship, and the beginning of a partnership. Let's talk SparkleSkin. Do we know anyone in Product Development over at Sephora?'
jokes.setup: Tom and Ann have officially ended their fake relationship
jokes.punchline: Tom instantly pivots from relationship post-mortem to business development — the romantic breakup becomes a corporate transition meeting
jokes.explanation: Tom treating a breakup as a business opportunity — 'the end of a relationship, the beginning of a partnership' — is his character in a sentence. The immediate 'Do we know anyone at Sephora?' grounds it in specific Tom-ness. Great economy.

jokes.text: Andy shows Leslie a series of photos: 'Here's a picture of me and April making out in her apartment. Here's a picture of us making out in Ben's office. This is us making out... I don't know where that is, but you can tell that she's sucking on my lip.'
jokes.setup: Andy is showing Leslie something on his phone (apparently to cheer her up about Ben)
jokes.punchline: It's an extended slideshow of Andy and April making out in various locations — the running commentary, including Andy's uncertainty about geography but certainty about lip-sucking, is the joke
jokes.explanation: The escalating list of makeout photo locations culminating in the genuinely confused 'I don't know where that is, but you can tell she's sucking on my lip' is a great Andy moment. His equal certainty about the anatomical detail and uncertainty about geography is perfectly character-specific.

jokes.text: Leslie's talking head about 'Hot Rebecca': 'I combined all of the giant, dark-haired smartphone power Goddesses into one woman called Hot Rebecca.'
jokes.setup: Leslie admits she's been distracted by jealousy about Ben's glamorous D.C. world
jokes.punchline: She has invented a composite jealousy figure named 'Hot Rebecca' — made up of all the women she fears Ben might prefer
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's best jokes. 'Hot Rebecca' as a jealousy amalgam is a genuinely original comedic concept — Leslie's anxiety given a specific name and form. 'Giant, dark-haired smartphone power Goddesses' is an inspired description of the D.C. women we've seen her intimidated by. The naming is perfect — 'Rebecca' is specific enough to be funny but generic enough to be universal. Highly quotable. Earns the 8+.

jokes.text: Andy trying to reassure Leslie: 'I know Ben, he, too, is an amalgam.' Leslie: 'No.' Andy: 'Yeah.' Leslie: 'Point is—' Andy: 'Nailed it.'
jokes.setup: Andy tries to reciprocate with his own 'amalgam' insight about Ben to make Leslie feel better
jokes.punchline: He has no idea what amalgam means — his use of the word is wrong, he knows it's wrong ('No.'), but he self-congratulates anyway with 'Nailed it.'
jokes.explanation: The callback to 'amalgam' — Andy misapplying the word he just heard, Leslie shutting it down with a single 'No.', and Andy's immediate 'Nailed it.' — is a tight three-beat structure. Andy's unsinkable confidence despite being wrong is his best recurring quality. Great economy.

jokes.text: Chris's talking head about the barbecue: 'My nomination was Jerry accidentally forwards his bank statement to everyone.' Ron: 'Classic. And depressing.'
jokes.setup: Ron sarcastically says he would have liked to see the puppet show about the funniest email chain
jokes.punchline: Chris reveals his nomination was Jerry's bank statement accidentally forwarded — Ron's response 'Classic. And depressing.' implies Jerry's finances are concerning
jokes.explanation: Ron's 'Classic. And depressing.' is perfectly Ron — a two-word assessment that simultaneously acknowledges the humor and the sadness of Jerry's situation. It's also a lovely economy: the adjective 'depressing' does enormous work without specifics. Dark Jerry joke landing cleanly.

jokes.text: Leslie sets up outdoor office hours at the polluted riverbank; immediately: 'Oh, my God. The smell is so much worse when you get up close.' Then Andy: 'Look. A handgun! I call it!'
jokes.setup: Leslie delivers an inspiring speech about cleaning up the river, setting up weekly office hours there
jokes.punchline: The inspirational moment is immediately undercut by the river's smell — then escalated to Andy finding and claiming a discarded handgun
jokes.explanation: A perfectly structured two-beat ending joke. Leslie's earnest declaration is first undercut by sensory reality (the smell), then completely demolished by Andy immediately claiming a discarded firearm with 'I call it!' — as if it's a prize. The escalation from inspirational to absurd to alarming in seconds is excellent writing. 'I call it!' for a handgun is a genuinely great line. Earns the 8+.

jokes.text: Ron's barbecue redemption: returns with proper meat, says simply 'Your work is appreciated. Eat some corn.' — then reveals Pig Tom has been slaughtered and cooked
jokes.setup: Ron abandoned the barbecue earlier in disgust; he returns with food and a brief acknowledgment
jokes.punchline: 'Also, here's Tom.' — revealing pig Tom has been processed and is now the ribs. Tom Haverford's horror at eating an animal with his name.
jokes.explanation: The payoff to the pig Tom setup is nearly perfect. Ron's economy — 'Also, here's Tom.' — does everything. The callback resolves naturally, Ron's philosophy has been vindicated, and Tom Haverford eating something named after him is a satisfying dark-comic button. 'Sorry, Tom.' as the group digs in is a great collective moment. Earns the 8+.

jokes.text: Leslie: 'There's only one sight I want to see right now.' [implies she means Ben] Ben: 'All right. I mean, this is getting weird. But, there it is.' Leslie: 'I meant the Jefferson Memorial, you perv!'
jokes.setup: Ben and Leslie have reconciled; Leslie sets up what sounds like a romantic/sexual statement
jokes.punchline: Leslie insists she meant the Jefferson Memorial — but then immediately agrees to the alternative reading: 'No, you didn't.' 'No, I didn't.'
jokes.explanation: A good misdirection with a satisfying extra beat — Leslie denies the reading, calls Ben a perv, then immediately admits she didn't mean the Jefferson Memorial. The 'No you didn't / No I didn't' exchange is a sweet, funny button on the couple's dynamic.

jokes.text: Andy as a tour guide: 'The White House, America's most whitest house. Most notably is where Sinbad lived in the film, First Kid.'
jokes.setup: Andy is apparently giving an impromptu tour of D.C.; he begins with the White House
jokes.punchline: 'Most whitest house' as a tautological description, then the 'most notable' fact being Sinbad's fictional residence in a 1996 kids movie
jokes.explanation: 'America's most whitest house' is a great tautological joke, but 'where Sinbad lived in the film First Kid' is the real gem. The specificity of First Kid (1996, Sinbad as a Secret Service agent) as the defining fact of the White House is inspired — it's exactly what Andy would consider most notable. Highly quotable, deeply character-integrated. Earns the 8+.

jokes.text: Leslie: 'Wait. No, you didn't.' Ben: 'No, I didn't.' Leslie: 'Spin it around and back it on up.'
jokes.setup: Leslie just told Ben he was being a perv for assuming she meant him.
jokes.punchline: Leslie immediately takes it back — she DID mean him. 'Spin it around and back it on up' as a romantic instruction.
jokes.explanation: 'Spin it around and back it on up' is a highly quotable and very Leslie phrase for indicating romantic interest. The three-beat structure of the full joke sequence (ambiguous setup, false denial, genuine admission with instruction) is excellent. High economy and character integration.

jokes.text: Other tourist: 'The other tour guide never said anything about that.' Andy: 'Do you know why it's called the Oval Office?' Tourist: 'No.' Andy: 'Because of a man. Oval Redenbacher. The popcorn inventor. He used to hang out with John F. Kennedy.'
jokes.setup: Andy is now attracting tourists with his confident misinformation; he poses a trivia question about the Oval Office
jokes.punchline: 'Oval Redenbacher' — a mashup of 'oval' (the shape) and 'Orville Redenbacher' (the popcorn mogul) — delivered as historical fact with JFK corroboration
jokes.explanation: The best joke in the episode. 'Oval Redenbacher' is a genuinely inspired wordplay that requires Andy to have (a) half-heard of Orville Redenbacher, (b) been looking for a reason the office is oval, and (c) connected them with complete confidence. 'The popcorn inventor. He used to hang out with John F. Kennedy.' adds a specific, verifiable-sounding detail that collapses immediately. The structure is perfect: trivia setup, confident false etymology, celebrity endorsement. Maximum economy. Meets the 8+ threshold comfortably — comparable to 'Never go with a hippie to a second location' in its unexpected specificity and quotability.

jokes.text: Leslie interrupts Andy's tour: 'Excuse me. Attention, everyone! This tour guide is the most amazing tour guide there ever was.' Andy: 'Please. Step up. $200 cash up front.'
jokes.setup: Leslie has been listening to Andy's tour and is impressed/horrified; she decides to endorse him publicly
jokes.punchline: Andy immediately charges $200 cash up front — he has now monetized his misinformation without missing a beat
jokes.explanation: Andy's instant entrepreneurship — '$200 cash up front' — without hesitation or self-doubt is a perfect button on the episode's closing joke sequence. Leslie's enablement of his nonsense is also very Leslie. The callback to the tour works well as an episode closer.

jokes.text: Andy's tourist speech: 'Excuse me. Attention, everyone! This tour guide is the most amazing tour guide there ever was. Please. Step up. $200 cash up front.'
jokes.setup: Andy has been giving an improvised and entirely fictional tour of D.C.
jokes.punchline: Andy's tourist is so impressed that they begin publicly advertising Andy's services — $200 cash upfront — turning his absurd misinformation tour into a business.
jokes.explanation: A good capper to the tour guide sequence. '$200 cash upfront' as the impromptu pricing for Andy's misinformation tour is funny. The escalation — from guy at monuments to charging tourists — pays off the bit well. The joke mainly works in the context of jokes #73 and #74.

tmdb_overview: Leslie and Andy visit Ben and April at their new jobs in Washington D.C., and Leslie feels overwhelmed by the city -- especially after meeting two of her idols. Meanwhile, Ron throws a "thank you" barbeque for the entire Parks and Recreation staff.
insight: Leslie's Washington move triggers 52 character-driven jokes but lands softer than peak Pawnee seasons.
